lessons.title: Essay Writing: Read the Task Before You Write

description.text: Turn an essay prompt into a clear audience, purpose, position and plan before drafting.

lessons.subject: english-language

objectives.statement: Identify genre, audience, purpose and required position in an essay prompt.
Build a logical position with paragraph-level reasons and examples.

text.text: Write an article for your school magazine arguing that students should complete community service before graduation. A good answer is not just a list of opinions: it must suit an article, address readers and defend a position.

Before writing, mark four things: the genre, the audience, the purpose and the command. Here the genre is an article, the audience is school readers, the purpose is to persuade, and the command is to argue for community service. Your plan should make each body paragraph perform a job rather than repeat the introduction.

items.text: Position: community service should be required, with sensible safeguards.
Reason 1: it develops responsibility through real contribution.
Reason 2: it connects school learning to community needs.
Qualification: the programme must be safe, supervised and accessible.

prompt.text: Turn the reason 'community service develops responsibility' into a paragraph plan.

steps.description: State the reason clearly: supervised service makes students responsible for a real task and its consequences.
Explain how arriving, completing duties and working with others practise responsibility; add a school or community example.
Connect the paragraph back to why the requirement benefits graduation.

answer.text: A paragraph needs a claim, explanation, concrete example and link—not merely the repeated phrase 'it teaches responsibility'.

text.text: Strong vocabulary cannot rescue an answer that ignores the genre, audience or question. Plan relevance first, then improve expression.

points.text: Give each paragraph one clear job.
Support claims with explanation and specific examples.

prompt.text: A prompt asks you to write a speech persuading parents to support a reading club. Which feature is essential?

content.text: Direct address and persuasive reasons suited to parents
A private diary entry with no audience
A list of unrelated definitions
Only a title and conclusion

feedback.text: A speech is spoken to an audience. The language and reasons must address the parents and persuade them.

hint.text: Use the genre and audience in the prompt.

prompt.text: Which outline best supports an argumentative essay?

content.text: Position, reason with evidence, second reason with evidence, qualification, conclusion
Definition, repeated opinion, repeated opinion, unrelated story
Conclusion first, then four disconnected examples
One paragraph containing every idea

feedback.text: The first outline creates a position, develops it logically and acknowledges a condition before concluding.

summary.text: A WAEC essay is judged by relevance, organisation and expression, not vocabulary alone.

lessons.title: Writing Forms: Letter, Report and Speech

description.text: Choose the form, voice and organisation that fit the reader and purpose.

lessons.subject: english-language

objectives.statement: Distinguish the structural and language features of a letter, report and speech.
Select an appropriate opening, tone and organisation for a specified audience.

text.text: You must inform a principal about broken laboratory equipment, persuade students to protect it, and tell a friend what happened. The facts may overlap, but the report, speech and informal letter cannot sound identical.

A report is factual, organised and addressed to a person or office. A speech is written to be heard, so it uses direct address, an opening greeting and persuasive rhythm. An informal letter uses a personal relationship and a natural conversational voice. Form is part of content: a response that sounds like the wrong genre loses control of the task.

rows: official reader; heading, facts, findings, recommendation
listeners; greeting, points, call to action
known friend or relative; personal sequence
content.alt: Comparison of report, speech and informal letter features.

prompt.text: You are writing a report to the principal about damaged laboratory stools. Which opening is most suitable?

steps.description: The report should identify the subject without sounding like a personal story.

steps.expression: REPORT ON THE CONDITION OF LABORATORY STOOLS
steps.description: A clear heading signals the form and subject.

steps.expression: On 12 May, the science club inspected...
steps.description: Begin with verifiable facts, then findings and recommendations.

answer.text: A report needs a clear subject, factual opening and organised findings; 'Dear best friend...' would belong to an informal letter, not this task.

text.text: Do not add a memorised heading or greeting without checking the task. The reader and purpose decide the form.

points.text: Identify the reader before choosing the voice.
Use the conventions that make the form recognisable.

prompt.text: Which feature most clearly belongs to a speech?

content.text: Greeting the audience and ending with a call to action
A confidential office heading and findings
A private address to a friend
A list of laboratory measurements only

feedback.text: A speech is designed to be heard by an audience, so greeting and direct appeal are characteristic features.

prompt.text: A report's recommendation should mainly be:

content.text: a practical action supported by the findings
a dramatic personal memory
a greeting to a friend
an unrelated proverb

feedback.text: A report moves from evidence to a reasonable action; the recommendation must follow its findings.

hint.text: What should an official reader be able to do next?

summary.text: Correct form makes purpose visible to the reader.

description.text: Answer exactly what the summary question demands using concise sentences in your own words.

objectives.statement: Select only the points that answer each part of a summary task.
Combine and paraphrase relevant points without changing their meaning.

text.text: A WAEC summary question may ask for two causes in two sentences and one remedy in one sentence. The passage may contain examples and explanations, but the answer must follow the number and type of points demanded.

Read the question before selecting points. Underline the exact causes, effects or remedies requested. Remove examples, repeated wording and attractive details that answer a different question. Then paraphrase: preserve the idea, change the wording, and keep the sentence grammatical.

items.text: Count the demanded points and sentences.
Mark only the passage clauses that answer the demand.
Combine related ideas without joining unrelated points.
Replace copied phrases and check that the meaning remains.

prompt.text: A passage asks for two human activities that degrade soil and one remedy. How should the response be organised?

steps.description: Give one clear cause in each sentence, rather than mixing both into a long paragraph.
Do not spend the remedy sentence repeating the causes.
Change the wording but retain the causal action and the proposed remedy.

answer.text: The response should contain two concise cause sentences and one concise remedy sentence. Its structure must mirror the task.

text.text: A sentence that contains a true but unrequested point does not earn the mark for the demanded point. Relevance beats volume.

points.text: Let the question determine what you select.
Paraphrase ideas, not merely individual words.
Match the required number and form of sentences.

prompt.text: If a question asks for two causes and one solution, which response plan is safest?

content.text: Two cause points and one solution point, each clearly expressed
Every interesting detail in the passage
One cause repeated three times
Only the solution because it is easiest

feedback.text: The response must answer every part of the demand and avoid replacing causes with unrelated details.

prompt.text: Which is the better summary style?

content.text: Concise sentences that preserve the passage's points in new wording
A long copy of the passage with a few words changed
Bullet points that ignore the requested sentence form
Personal opinions added to the writer's points

feedback.text: A summary selects relevant points, paraphrases them and obeys the requested form without adding opinion.

summary.text: Summary is controlled selection and paraphrase, not copying or shortening at random.

lessons.title: Comprehension: Tone, Attitude and Implied Meaning

description.text: Use word choice, comparisons and contrast to infer how a writer feels and what the passage implies.

lessons.subject: english-language

objectives.statement: Infer an attitude from several language choices rather than one isolated word.
Distinguish literal information from the writer's implied evaluation.

text.text: A writer who calls a policy 'a brave attempt' is not necessarily praising it completely. The surrounding sentences may reveal approval, doubt or irony. Tone comes from the pattern of language, not from one adjective alone.

First identify what happened literally. Then examine loaded words, comparisons, contrast and what the writer chooses to praise or criticise. An inference is safe only when more than one clue supports it. Avoid answers that turn mild doubt into anger or a single concern into total rejection.

prompt.text: A writer describes a new transport plan as 'ambitious but poorly explained'. What attitude is most supported?

steps.description: The writer recognises a positive goal.
The contrast identifies a serious weakness.
The safest attitude is mixed or cautiously critical, not complete praise or hatred.

answer.text: The writer is cautiously critical: the goal is respected, but the explanation is judged inadequate.

text.text: When two tone options seem possible, quote or identify the words that support each. The stronger answer explains the whole pattern.

points.text: Separate literal event from implied evaluation.
Use repeated language and contrast to infer attitude.

prompt.text: A writer calls a failed project 'an expensive lesson' and recommends a better plan. The tone is best described as:

content.text: reflective and cautiously constructive
joyfully celebratory
completely indifferent
personally abusive

feedback.text: Expensive lesson shows criticism, while recommending a better plan shows constructive reflection. The extreme options overstate the tone.

hint.text: Combine the criticism with the recommendation.

prompt.text: Which evidence is strongest for an inference about a writer's attitude?

content.text: Several repeated evaluative words and a concluding recommendation
One unfamiliar word taken alone
The reader's personal experience
A fact from another subject

feedback.text: A pattern within the passage provides stronger evidence than one word or outside knowledge.

summary.text: Tone is an evidence-based reading of the writer's evaluation.
